lead: Validation asks one question: is this the system the customer actually needs? A careful read of the SRS catches an ambiguous, missing or conflicting requirement while the fix is still one sentence. Management keeps every later change visible: each requirement has a version, a baseline, a change record and links to design and tests. A UPI app that adds a cancellation fee two months after launch needs the old requirements intact and the new ones traceable.
prereq: You need the requirement types from 2.1 and the elicited stakeholder needs from 2.3.

blocks.text: Validation asks whether the written requirements describe the system the user needs. Verification asks whether the built system matches them. Validation works on the document, before design; verification runs on code (Unit 4).
Four techniques find defects while a fix is still a sentence:

items: Inspection: three to five people read the SRS against a checklist and log each defect with its requirement number.
Prototyping: an unclear screen becomes a throwaway model shown to users; their reaction becomes the rewritten requirement.
Test-case generation: write one acceptance test per requirement; if no test can be written, the requirement is not testable.

Checklist: ambiguity (each requirement has only one possible reading), completeness (every input, output, error, constraint), consistency (no two requirements contradict), testability (something measurable, numbers carry units).

blocks.text: A baseline is a reviewed SRS frozen under a version label, v1.0. After that it changes only through a numbered change request (CR) that states the change and its reason.

items: Log CR-01 in the change register: date, requester, reason.
Impact analysis: affected requirements, design modules, code units, test cases, effort in person-days, schedule.
Change control board (product owner, lead designer, test lead) approves, rejects or defers.
An approved change is edited in, re-reviewed and released as v1.1; the v1.0 baseline is kept.
Traceability matrix and requirement status are updated.

blocks.text: Only a few universities examine the formal board procedure in detail.
A traceability matrix has one row per requirement and columns for design and test, so a change shows exactly which module and test must move. Status runs proposed, approved, implemented, verified.

figure.caption: Each change request passes through impact analysis and a board decision before a new baseline exists.

spec.title: From baseline to baseline
spec.aria: A downward chain from SRS v1.0 through change request CR-01, impact analysis on 5 modules, change board decision, approved change, to new baseline SRS v1.1.

examples.question: An SRS holds 40 numbered requirements. A validation inspection logs 6 ambiguous requirements, 3 missing requirements and 2 conflicting pairs. After the first baseline, change request CR-01 asks for a cancellation fee; impact analysis traces it to 5 design modules. (a) How many defects must be fixed before the first baseline, and how many of the original requirements are clean? (b) State the management steps for CR-01.
steps: The 3 missing requirements are new and will be added. The 2 conflicting pairs touch 4 of the existing 40, so 6 + 4 = 10 of them carry defects and 30 are clean.
Each defect is logged by requirement number, fixed by the author and re-inspected until the count is zero; the SRS is then baselined as v1.0 with 43 requirements.
CR-01 is logged with ID, requester and reason, then costed by impact analysis over requirements, 5 design modules and new test case T-13.
The board approves or rejects; on approval the SRS is re-reviewed, released as v1.1, and row R13 is added to the matrix.
examples.answer: 11 defects; 30 of the original 40 requirements were clean; v1.0 is baselined with 43 requirements. CR-01 touches 5 modules and, once approved, becomes v1.1 with R13 traceable to design and test.
examples.check:
ambiguous, missing, conflicting = 6, 3, 2
conflicting_reqs = 4
defects = ambiguous + missing + conflicting
clean = 40 - (ambiguous + conflicting_reqs)
total = 40 + missing
print(defects, clean, total)

traps: Validation is not testing the code; running tests against code is verification (Unit 4).
A change accepted without impact analysis, or without a new baseline version, leaves design and tests silently out of date.
Do not mix the defect kinds: an ambiguous requirement exists but reads two ways, a missing one is absent, conflicting ones contradict each other.
Traceability matrix rows are requirements, not modules.

quiz.a: A reviewed and approved version of a work product such as the SRS, kept under change control so later edits need a change request.

quiz.q: Name two items on a requirements validation checklist.
quiz.a: Any two of: ambiguity, completeness, consistency, testability.
Validation asks whether the requirements describe the system the user needs, and works on the document. Verification asks whether the built system matches the requirements, and works on code.

quiz.q: An SRS has 60 requirements. A review logs 8 ambiguous, 4 missing and 3 conflicting requirements. Find the defect count and the number of clean requirements.
quiz.a: Defects = 8 + 4 + 3 = 15. The 8 ambiguous and 3 conflicting requirements are among the 60, so 11 of them carry defects and 49 are clean. After the 4 missing ones are added the SRS holds 64 clean requirements.

quiz.q: R14 refund was baselined in v1.0, but its test case was deleted by mistake. State the management action.
quiz.a: Because R14 is under baseline v1.0, the new test is raised as a change request, impact-analysed and approved, then released as v1.1 with the matrix and status updated.

quiz.q: Why must impact analysis come before the change board decision?
quiz.a: The board can only approve, reject or defer if it knows the cost: affected requirements, modules, tests, effort and schedule. Without it, approval is a guess and design and tests drift from the SRS.

quiz.q: "The app must respond quickly." Which checklist items fail, and how do you rewrite it?
quiz.a: Ambiguity and testability fail: there is no measure. Rewrite as: "Search results appear within 2 seconds for 95% of queries on a 4G connection."

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry keeps requirements in an issue tracker, so each item has an ID, a status field and links to commits and test runs, and the matrix is generated rather than drawn by hand. Safety standards in avionics and medical devices demand bidirectional traceability. Research chases automatic detection of vague wording and requirements smells. Useful search terms: requirements traceability matrix, change control board.
